title: Nelson Puts the Telescope to His Blind Eye
text:
On April 2, 1801, a British fleet attacked the Danish fleet and shore batteries at Copenhagen. Vice Admiral Horatio Nelson led the attacking squadron into the narrow channel, while the commander in chief, Admiral Sir Hyde Parker, watched from farther away with the heavier ships.

The fighting was fierce, and several British ships ran aground. Parker, unable to see clearly how the battle was going, hoisted signal 39, ordering the fleet to discontinue the action.

Colonel William Stewart, who was beside Nelson on his flagship, wrote an account of what happened next. Nelson was told of the signal and asked whether his own signal for close action was still flying. He ordered it kept up. Then he turned to his flag captain, Thomas Foley, and said he had only one eye and had a right to be blind sometimes. He raised his telescope to his blind eye and said he really did not see the signal.

Nelson kept fighting. Within a few hours the Danish line was largely silenced, and Nelson negotiated a truce. He was later made a viscount.
lesson: The person closest to the problem often sees it best. Know the purpose behind an order well enough to judge when following it would defeat it.
people: Horatio Nelson, Sir Hyde Parker, Thomas Foley, William Stewart
source: Colonel William Stewart's account, printed in Clarke and M'Arthur, The Life of Admiral Lord Nelson (1809); Robert Southey, The Life of Nelson
caveat: Some historians think Parker meant the signal as permission to withdraw at Nelson's discretion, and that the telescope scene was partly a joke.
